original_value: Novices learn innovation best through project-based learning (PBL), working in face-to-face teams to tackle real-world problems. Yet, real-world projects are complex, stressful, and especially challenging for novices. Online communities could provide social support to motivate novices, but it is unclear how to design online communities to support face-to-face PBL teams. Here we ask:How might we design an online system that enlists external supporters to provide online social support to motivate PBL students?Our need-finding study found that PBL students received infrequent social support, rarely engaged in help-seeking, and perceived little progress until the end of their projects. Based on these findings, we designedCheerOn, an online social support system that prompts novice student teams to externalize progress allowing external, online supporters to offer social support. We testedCheerOnwith 3 PBL teams and 15 external supporters over a 6-week course. We found that external supporters provided instrumental, informational, and emotional support that strengthened students’ bonds to the community, which increased help-seeking. Supporters also provided appraisal support, which increased students’ perceived value of their work. Supporters were more likely to offer informational and instrumental support when they were promoted or saw a clear need for help; supporters who received gratitude from students were more likely to offer emotional support in return; and supporters who were closely connected to the community were more likely how offer appraisal and instrumental support. Theoretically, this research contributes to our understanding of how hybrid face-to-face and online communities can impact the behavior of PBL students, specifically towards the facilitation of help-seeking behavior, as well as increased understanding of to different types of social support (i.e., appraisal, emotional, informational, and instrumental) can impact the participation of PBL students and supporters. Practically, this research contributes to our understanding of how to design socio-technical systems that facilitate social support for offline novice PBL students working, expanding the instructional resources available for preparing novices in PBL environments.

result.paraphrase: Novices learn innovation best through project-based learning (PBL), where face-to-face teams tackle real-world problems. However, such projects are complex, stressful, and particularly difficult for novices. Online communities may offer social support to motivate novices, but how to design them for face-to-face PBL teams remains unclear. We therefore ask: How might we design an online system that enlists external supporters to provide online social support to motivate PBL students? Our need-finding study showed that PBL students received social support infrequently, seldom sought help, and felt little progress until their projects ended. Drawing on these findings, we created CheerOn, an online social support system that encourages novice student teams to make progress visible so external online supporters can provide social support. We evaluated CheerOn with 3 PBL teams and 15 external supporters during a 6-week course. We found that external supporters offered instrumental, informational, and emotional support, strengthening students’ connection to the community and increasing help-seeking. Supporters also provided appraisal support, which increased students’ perceived value of their work. Supporters were more likely to give informational and instrumental support when prompted or when they saw a clear need for help; supporters who received gratitude from students were more likely to respond with emotional support; and supporters who were closely connected to the community were more likely to offer appraisal and instrumental support. Theoretically, this research deepens understanding of how hybrid face-to-face and online communities affect PBL student behavior, especially in facilitating help-seeking, and of how different forms of social support (appraisal, emotional, informational, and instrumental) shape participation by PBL students and supporters. Practically, it improves understanding of how to design socio-technical systems that facilitate social support for offline novice PBL students, expanding the instructional resources available for preparing novices in PBL environments.
